::: {#brief .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-sb-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The brief</p>
<dl class="lx-sb-facts">
<div><dt>The city</dt><dd>Prairie City (fictional): <b>250,000 people</b> in a dense core, suburbs and a rural fringe, each behind <b>one <span class="lx-term" data-term="substation">substation</span></b> (a teaching simplification); 2025's homes, prices and eight representative days.</dd></div>
<div><dt>You decide</dt><dd>How many furnaces become <span class="lx-term" data-term="heat-pump">heat pumps</span>; <span class="lx-term" data-term="retrofit">retrofits</span>; a <span class="lx-term" data-term="district-heating">district-heat</span> network in the core; <span class="lx-term" data-term="electric-vehicle">electric cars (EVs)</span> and how they charge; rooftop solar; batteries; whether substations may be upgraded.</dd></div>
<div><dt>The engine works out</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="linear-program">linear program (LP)</span> runs the city's <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-hub">energy hub</span> hour by hour at the least cost, each hour within each substation's limit, and buys upgrades only where the busiest hour needs them.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Who pays</dt><dd>Bills by household group and their <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">energy burden</span>: home energy bills as a share of income. Groups are bands of <span class="lx-term" data-term="area-median-income">area median income (AMI)</span>.</dd></div>
<div><dt>It leaves out</dt><dd>Power flow inside a district, outages, growth to 2040, the cars' prices, and how bills are really set: the household table is a <span class="lx-term" data-term="screening-estimate">screening estimate</span>, not an output of the LP.</dd></div>
<div><dt>It assumes</dt><dd>Every heat pump is large enough for the coldest modeled hour: equipment sizes and their limits are not modeled.</dd></div>
</dl>
<p class="lx-hint">Open-ended: start from a preset, change one thing at a time, and copy the plan link to keep a plan. Prairie City is fictional; its numbers are illustrative.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Siting with map layers is in the capstone <a href="c3-prairie-city-2040.html">C3</a>: the same engine, with <a href="a19-gis-siting.html">A19</a>'s map for a solar farm.</p>
</div>
```

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## How the engine works, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="sb3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>The hub</dt><dd>Each hour, electricity through the substation, gas and rooftop sun must meet each district's heat, base load and car charging; heat pumps, furnaces, a heat network, batteries and managed charging sit between.</dd>
<dt>The limit</dt><dd>Each substation's flow stays below its limit every hour, unless the plan buys more room; the busiest hour decides, not the year's total.</dd>
<dt>It holds when</dt><dd>Eight representative days stand for 2025, storage shifts energy only within a day, and 2025's prices, people and homes stay as they are.</dd>
<dt>The full-year check</dt><dd>The presets, run again on every hour of 2025: total yearly cost and CO₂ within 0.1% (the change against 2025 moves by a little more).</dd>
<dt>What it tests</dt><dd>The year is scaled, like the days, to the same annual heat and base energy, so the totals agree partly by construction: it checks the hours' timing.</dd>
<dt>Cold days in the year</dt><dd>The tightest hours fall on 19 or 20 February, two other days the design day stands for; plans that buy upgrades need a little more room.</dd>
<dt>Who pays</dt><dd>Bills and energy burden by household group come from an accounting layer after the LP, with a stated rule for who adopts first.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The linear program behind the bench</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The formulation:** [M12](m12-city-model.html) writes the hub down, with building shares as decisions, the balance in each district-hour and the substation's ceiling.
- **Its duals:** the ceiling's dual is the value of more room; a CO₂ cap's dual is the cost of the last tonne.
- **The notebook:** M12's rebuilds the model in Python with SciPy and HiGHS.
- **The capstone:** [C3](c3-prairie-city-2040.html) plans the city to 2040 on this engine.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>When two answers cost the same: the tie rule</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>With one electricity price all day, many schedules cost the same: a car can charge at 01:00 or 03:00. Small stated costs pick one; they are left out of every reported cost total, but the LP's duals include them:</p>
<ul class="sb3-rules">
<li>$20 a year per MW of each district's busiest hour, and $10 per MW of the three districts' busiest hour together: flexible loads spread out.</li>
<li>$1 per MWh out of a battery and $0.50 per MWh out of the heat store: no cycling for nothing.</li>
<li>$0.10 per MWh of managed charging, times the hour's share of SPP's peak demand: quieter hours first.</li>
</ul>
<p>So the LP minimizes the cost plus these small costs. On a few plans it pays a little to keep a busiest hour that is under its limit lower:</p>
<ul class="sb3-rules">
<li><b>The price of the ties:</b> under $30 a year in the engine's test, against the cheapest schedule found without them.</li>
<li><b>The same answer:</b> every preset run again with the costs ×2 and ×0.1 gives the same numbers.</li>
<li><b>One answer:</b> each busiest hour, upgrade and the energy bought stays within the test's tolerances (0.5 MW, 0.05 MW and 5 MWh) over all plans within $1 of the best cost.</li>
<li><b>The duals:</b> where a limit binds without an upgrade, the reported cost saves about $9 per MW a year more than the dual shows: the tie costs' share.</li>
<li><b>Your plans:</b> not checked this way; their hourly schedules can still differ.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
